summary: There is exactly ONE cron job on live prod (jobid 2, `*/5 * * * *`, POST to /api/cron) and it is the sole source of all 29,250 lifetime `net.http_post` calls — no trigger or function makes egress calls. So "cron scheduling" is really one question: is a 5-minute tick worth what it costs? The answer is that the tick itself is cheap, but everything hanging off it is not — 2.1 s of DB time is spent per tick just deciding what to run (62 h/yr), each per-type claim scans 30.7 MB of buffers because of a non-sargable predicate, six sweeps mint 1,722 job rows/day against 696 completions, and one tick job (`email_send`) burns 31.7 s of the 50 s budget per attempt on a dead SMTP socket. Worst of all, the retry sweep it feeds has no write-back, so it re-sent the same 4 emails 763 times in 24 h and actually delivered 194 duplicate verification emails to one real address before exhausting the provider's daily quota. Separately, 36% of the 241 MB production database (86 MB) is pure scheduler exhaust — `cron.job_run_details` (46 MB, no retention, structurally invisible to autovacuum) and `net._http_response` (40 MB of bloat holding 72 live rows) — recoverable with zero code change. I also correct a banked figure: the pg_net cleanup's 2.6 h is historical debt, not a live drain (measured marginal cost now is 12 ms/call, not 129 ms).

findings.title: email_retry_failed re-sends the same failed emails forever — 763 attempts in 24h for 4 emails, 194 duplicates actually delivered to one real user, provider daily quota exhausted
findings.evidence: lib/services/scheduler.service.ts:72-104 — `retryFailedEmails()` does `SELECT * FROM email_logs WHERE status='failed' AND created_at >= NOW()-INTERVAL '24 hours' ... LIMIT 50`, calls `sendTemplatedEmail` per row, and NEVER writes back to email_logs (no retried_at, no status change, no counter). The same rows are therefore re-selected on every run for a full 24 hours, and each failed retry inserts a NEW 'failed' row that itself enters the window. Live prod, last 24h, `SELECT status, template_key, count(*) FROM email_logs WHERE created_at > now()-interval '24 hours' GROUP BY 1,2`: group_verification_link 490 failed / 196 queued / 194 SENT (all 194 sends between 00:00:07 and 00:25:11 — i.e. 194 duplicate verification emails delivered to one address in 25 minutes), staff_operational_alert 204 failed, weekly_summary 55 failed, account_statement 14 failed. Recipients: `SELECT "to", count(*) ... GROUP BY 1` returns exactly FOUR addresses (ezrawafula98@gmail.com 490, support@kitabuyetu.co.ke 204, wanyonyipolycarp@gmail.com 57, Midevabritney@gmail.com 12). error_message values include 'You have reached your daily email sending quota.' — the loop consumed the paid provider quota on duplicates. 761 failed rows currently sit inside the 24h retry window; email_logs holds 42,895 failed rows / 21 MB total.
findings.impact: A real user received ~194 identical verification emails in 25 minutes (deliverability/spam-complaint risk on a domain that just came out of a 14-day outage). The paid email provider's daily quota is being burned on ~763 duplicate attempts/day for 4 unique messages. It generates ~800 new 'failed' email_logs rows/day which feed themselves back into the window, and it is the single largest job_queue consumer (4,492 pending, 897 rows carrying 'Timed out in processing; reset by stuck-job sweep', ZERO completions in 24h since 2026-08-20).
findings.recommendation: Add a `retry_attempted_at timestamptz` (or `retry_count int`) column to email_logs and have `retryFailedEmails()` stamp every row it touches, then add `AND retry_attempted_at IS NULL` to the SELECT. That alone converts an unbounded loop into at-most-once. Also skip rows whose error_message indicates a permanent condition (quota exceeded, invalid recipient) instead of retrying them, and cap total retries per row at 1-2. Until it is fixed, the type should be disabled — it is delivering spam and burning quota, not recovering mail.

findings.title: email_send burns 31.7 s of the 50 s tick budget per attempt on a dead SMTP socket — 75% of ALL job execution time in 24h for 2 successful sends
findings.evidence: Live prod, `SELECT q.type, count(*), avg(l.duration_ms), max(l.duration_ms), sum(l.duration_ms)/1000 FROM job_logs l JOIN job_queue q ON q.id=l.job_id WHERE l.created_at > now()-interval '24 hours' AND l.duration_ms IS NOT NULL GROUP BY 1`: email_send = 104 log rows, avg 31,705 ms, max 32,864 ms, total 3,297 s. The next-largest is mpesa_daily_report at 332 s; the sum across ALL 15 types is 4,384 s, so email_send is 75.2%. Outcome for the same 24h (`SELECT type,status,count(*),(array_agg(DISTINCT left(last_error,180)))[1:2] FROM job_queue ...`): email_send = 2 completed, 19 failed, last_error 'Greeting never received' (an SMTP banner timeout, i.e. the connection opens and the server never speaks). Tick budget is `TIME_BUDGET_MS = 50_000` at lib/jobs/processor.ts:72; `MIN_JOB_BUDGET_MS = 10_000` at lib/jobs/processor.ts:~85. A single email_send attempt therefore consumes 63% of a tick.
findings.impact: Every tick that draws an email_send job loses ~32 of its 50 usable seconds to a socket that will never answer, then the round-robin at lib/jobs/processor.ts:147-166 has ~8 s left for ~11 other pending types. This is a direct, measured cause of the starvation Sentry reports as KITABUYETU-1 and of the observed ~5 completions per tick against a BATCH_SIZE of 100. ~3,297 s/day = 55 min/day of Vercel function time billed for nothing.
findings.recommendation: Put a hard socket/connect timeout on the SMTP transport (5 s connect, 10 s total) so a dead endpoint costs 5 s not 32 s, and wrap the send in the tick deadline already published by `setTickDeadline` (lib/jobs/deadline.ts) so a handler refuses to start a send it cannot finish. Add a circuit breaker: after N consecutive 'Greeting never received' failures, fail the job fast for a cooldown window instead of re-dialling. The underlying dead SMTP fallback is a separate correctness issue but the timeout is the optimization fix and is independent of it.

findings.title: Six 5-minute sweeps still use time-bucketed dedup keys and mint 1,722 job rows/day against 696 completions — the entire queue growth, with the fix already proven on four sibling types in the same file
findings.evidence: lib/jobs/index.ts:62-148. Six types carry `dedup_key: '<type>:${dateStr}T${hour}:${fiveMinBucket}'` — email_campaign_process (:62-65), email_retry_failed (:67-70), email_campaign_drain (:76-79), mpesa_reconcile (:133-136), mpesa_replay_callbacks (:139-142), outbox_dispatch (:145-148) — so a NEW row is minted every tick whether or not the previous one ever ran. Four sibling sweeps at lib/jobs/index.ts:111-131 were converted to CONSTANT dedup keys and the comment at lines 81-106 explains exactly why; lines 107-110 state the mpesa_*/outbox_* sweeps were deliberately left alone ('they have the same shape and probably want the same treatment... not changed blind'). Live prod measurement of both groups, `SELECT type, count(*) FILTER (WHERE created_at > now()-'24h') AS enq, count(*) FILTER (WHERE status='completed' AND updated_at > now()-'24h') AS done, count(*) FILTER (WHERE status='pending') AS pending FROM job_queue GROUP BY 1` — TIME-BUCKETED (broken): email_retry_failed 287/0/4,491; outbox_dispatch 287/159/2,091; email_campaign_drain 287/151/3,650; email_campaign_process 287/129/3,588; mpesa_replay_callbacks 287/141/2,416; mpesa_reconcile 287/116/2,765. CONSTANT-KEY CONTROL (healthy): sms_retry_failed 175/174/1; sms_release_stale_reservations 92/91/1; sms_poll_dlr 71/70/1; sms_process_schedules 62/61/1. The control group's enqueue count self-throttles to its completion rate and pending never exceeds 1.
findings.impact: 1,722 enqueued/day vs 696 completed/day = +1,026 permanently-undrainable job_queue rows every day, which is the whole of the queue's growth (18,264 -> 19,006 pending observed this session). Those 19,001 rows are what makes every claim and every depth query expensive (see the claim-scan and per-tick-overhead findings), so the enqueue bug is upstream of most of the tick's cost. At 425 B/row that is ~155 MB/yr of table growth on a 241 MB database.
findings.recommendation: Change the six dedup_key expressions at lib/jobs/index.ts:62-148 to bare constants ('email_retry_failed', 'outbox_dispatch', ...), exactly as at lines 111-131. The partial unique index idx_job_queue_dedup (dedup_key WHERE status NOT IN ('completed','failed')) then enforces at-most-one-outstanding-per-type, and resetStuckJobs(6) already guarantees the key frees itself. All six are self-idempotent sweeps that claim whatever is due when they run, so a suppressed enqueue loses nothing. Then one-off DELETE the ~19,000 orphaned pending rows.

findings.title: pg_net timeout is 20 s against a 60 s function — 100% of cron HTTP responses are discarded timeouts, while cron.job_run_details reports 29,244 of 29,244 runs 'succeeded'
findings.evidence: cron.job jobid 2 command passes `timeout_milliseconds := 20000`. app/api/cron/route.ts:38 sets `export const maxDuration = 60` and lib/jobs/processor.ts:72 sets `TIME_BUDGET_MS = 50_000` — the route's own comment at lines 28-37 reasons about '60s leaves 10s of headroom over the batch budget' while the actual client gives up at 20 s. Live: `SELECT status_code, timed_out, count(*), min(created), max(created) FROM net._http_response GROUP BY 1,2` returns exactly ONE row — status_code NULL, timed_out TRUE, count 72, covering 06:55 to 12:50 UTC 2026-09-04, i.e. every retained response. Sample error_msg: 'Timeout of 20000 ms reached. Total time: 20001.961000 ms (DNS time: 118.112000 ms, TCP/SSL handshake time: 72.805000 ms, HTTP Request/Response time: 19807.788000 ms)'. Meanwhile `SELECT count(*), count(*) FILTER (WHERE status='succeeded') FROM cron.job_run_details` = 29,244 / 29,244, because net.http_post returns a request id synchronously and pg_cron only records that. FALSIFICATION: the work is NOT truncated — completion offsets within the tick reach 54 s (`SELECT max(EXTRACT(epoch FROM updated_at)::bigint % 300) FROM job_queue WHERE status='completed'` grouped by type: mpesa_daily_report 54, email_campaign_drain 45, sms_retry_failed 44), so Vercel keeps running past the client disconnect.
findings.impact: Nothing in the system can ever observe a 401, a 500, a bad CRON_SECRET, or a failed deploy on the scheduler's only entry point — the response body is thrown away 100% of the time and the only run log says 'succeeded'. pg_stat_statements still contains someone's forensic probe for exactly this ('Bypass the Vault entirely; embed the literal secret... If 200 -> Vault has the wrong value. If 401 -> Vercel has a different value'), which is what diagnosing a scheduler with no feedback costs. Secondary: 288 x 20 s = 96 minutes/day of pg_net worker slot held on a response that is discarded.
findings.recommendation: Either raise `timeout_milliseconds` to 60000 so the response is captured (cheapest — one cron.unschedule/cron.schedule), or better, make POST /api/cron return 202 immediately after kicking off the batch so pg_net records a real status code in ~200 ms. Then add a cheap health check that alerts when net._http_response contains no 2xx for the last hour. Do NOT reduce the tick frequency to compensate — see the throughput findings; the tick is already the constraint.

findings.title: cron.job_run_details is 46 MB with no retention AND is structurally invisible to autovacuum — 19% of the production database, growing 467 KB/day
findings.evidence: `SELECT count(*), min(start_time), pg_size_pretty(pg_total_relation_size('cron.job_run_details')), pg_total_relation_size(...)/count(*) AS bytes_per_row, avg(length(command)) FROM cron.job_run_details` = 29,245 rows, oldest 2026-05-25 23:50:00, 46 MB, 1,660 bytes/row, avg command length 460 bytes (the full inline SQL of the job is stored on EVERY run), avg return_message 5 bytes. `SELECT ... FROM pg_stat_all_tables WHERE schemaname='cron'` shows n_tup_ins=0, n_live_tup=0, last_vacuum NULL, last_autovacuum NULL, last_analyze NULL, autovacuum_count 0 — pg_cron's launcher writes these rows without them appearing in the table's insert statistics, so the autovacuum daemon sees no work and will NEVER trigger. Corroborating: `SELECT relpages, reltuples FROM pg_class` gives relpages=0, reltuples=-1 (never analyzed in the table's life). There is no purge job — `SELECT count(*) FROM cron.job` = 1, and that one job is the 5-minute HTTP post. cron.log_run and cron.log_statement are both 'on' (defaults). Growth: 46 MB / 102 days = 467 KB/day = 167 MB/year.
findings.impact: 46 MB of the 241 MB production database (19.1%) is a log of one cron job posting to one URL, retained forever, in every backup and every restore. Combined with net._http_response's 40 MB it is 35.9% of the database (measured: `round(100.0*(pg_total_relation_size('cron.job_run_details')+pg_total_relation_size('net._http_response'))/pg_database_size(current_database()),1)` = 35.9). It will pass the real business data (9 groups, 49 payments, 23 contributions) in size several times over each year, and because autovacuum can never touch it the on-disk cost is 1,660 B for ~530 B of content.
findings.recommendation: Schedule a second cron job for retention, e.g. `cron.schedule('purge-cron-history','17 3 * * *', $$DELETE FROM cron.job_run_details WHERE end_time < now() - interval '7 days'$$)` — Supabase's own documented pattern. Then run one VACUUM (FULL) cron.job_run_details to return the ~43 MB (7 days = ~2,016 rows = ~3.3 MB retained). Because autovacuum never fires here, the purge job must be paired with an explicit periodic VACUUM or the space is marked free but never reclaimed.

findings.title: Per-type job claim uses a non-sargable `($2 IS NULL OR type = $2)` predicate — 3,924 shared blocks (30.7 MB) touched per claim, ~106 GB/day of buffer traffic, and it scales linearly with tick frequency
findings.evidence: lib/jobs/db.ts:30-49, specifically line 40: `AND ($2::text IS NULL OR type = $2)`. No index can serve that OR form even if one existed on `type`. The only pick index is `idx_job_queue_pick ON job_queue (priority DESC, run_at) WHERE status='pending'` (`SELECT pg_get_indexdef(indexrelid) FROM pg_stat_all_indexes WHERE relname='job_queue'`) — it has no `type` column, so a claim for a low-priority type walks every higher-priority pending row and heap-fetches each to test `type`. Live cost, `SELECT calls, mean_exec_time, shared_blks_hit FROM pg_stat_statements WHERE query ILIKE '%job_queue%'` for the typed claim `UPDATE job_queue SET status=$3 ... AND ($2::text IS NULL OR type=$2) ORDER BY priority DESC, run_at ASC LIMIT $1 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`: 21,255 calls, shared_blks_hit 83,400,706 = 3,924 blocks (30.7 MB) per call, mean 6.6 ms, max 1,963.7 ms. That is the single largest shared-buffer consumer in the database — larger than the pg_net cleanup's 80.4M. processJobBatch calls it once per type per round (lib/jobs/processor.ts:157), and there are ~11-12 distinct pending types, so ~12 claims per tick.
findings.impact: ~12 claims/tick x 288 ticks/day x 3,924 blocks = 13.6M blocks/day ≈ 106 GB/day of buffer traffic purely to pick jobs. The cost is proportional to the pending backlog (19,006 rows concentrated in 6 types), so it compounds with the enqueue-amplification finding: the more the queue grows, the more expensive each claim, which is the mechanism behind the observed max of 1,963.7 ms on what should be a sub-millisecond lookup. It also puts a floor under how often the tick can affordably run.
findings.recommendation: Split the query into two statements (typed and untyped) instead of the `$2 IS NULL OR` form, and add `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_job_queue_pick_type ON job_queue (type, priority DESC, run_at) WHERE status='pending'`. The typed claim then becomes a ~5-block index lookup, cutting the 106 GB/day to roughly 17 MB/day. Fixing the enqueue amplification first shrinks the backlog and reduces the cost independently, but the index is what makes it O(1) rather than O(backlog).

findings.title: net._http_response holds 5,075 heap pages for 72 live rows and has been autovacuumed exactly once in its life — and the banked 2.6-hour cleanup cost is historical debt, not a live drain
findings.evidence: `SELECT relpages, reltuples, pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size(oid)) FROM pg_class WHERE oid='net._http_response'::regclass` = 5,075 pages / 72 tuples / 40 MB — ~70 pages per live row, ~99.6% empty. `pg_stat_all_tables`: last_autovacuum 2026-08-05 09:53:50, autovacuum_count 1, last_vacuum NULL, vacuum_count 0, n_tup_ins 29,250 / n_tup_del 29,178 across both stat buckets. CORRECTION TO THE BANKED FIGURE, measured this session: two pg_stat_statements samples of queryid 5704065269939664754 taken 4 min 1 s apart — 12:56:57 (calls 72,704, total_ms 9,412,119, blks 80,395,895) and 13:00:58 (calls 72,706, total_ms 9,412,143, blks 80,395,949) — give a MARGINAL cost of +2 calls, +24 ms, +54 blocks = 12 ms and 27 blocks per call, against a lifetime mean of 129 ms and 1,106 blocks per call. Confirmed by plan: `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` of the cleanup's CTE today is 'Index Only Scan using _http_response_created_idx ... Buffers: shared hit=29, Execution Time: 0.246 ms'. Lifetime totals stand at 72,706 calls / 9,412,143 ms (2.61 h) / 80.4M blocks (643 GB) to delete 29,179 rows; stddev 385 ms and max 4,143 ms show that total is dominated by a minority of very slow calls, i.e. the cleanup queued behind the same overloaded DB the job queue creates.
findings.impact: The 2.6 h is real DB time already spent but it is NOT accruing at that rate — reporting it as a live 2.6-hour drain would misdirect the fix. What IS live: 40 MB (16.6% of the 241 MB database) of permanently allocated empty heap that is in every backup, and a table whose bloat re-inflates the cleanup's cost whenever the DB is under load (max 4,143 ms observed). pg_net.ttl is the default '6 hours' and batch_size 200, so the steady state is only ~72 rows — the 5,075 pages can never be repopulated and will never be reclaimed by ordinary autovacuum.
findings.recommendation: Run `VACUUM (FULL) net._http_response` once — it is 40 MB and 72 live rows, so it takes seconds and returns ~40 MB. Combined with the cron.job_run_details purge that is 82.7 MB (34% of the database) recovered with zero code change. Optionally set `pg_net.ttl` to '1 hour' (12 retained rows at this call volume) so the table cannot re-bloat. Do NOT prioritise this as a CPU fix — its current CPU cost is ~8.6 s/day.

findings.title: Two of the six 5-minute sweeps drive tables that have NEVER held a single row — 574 jobs/day, 209,510/year, 7,239 pending, for provably zero work
findings.evidence: Live prod: `SELECT count(*) FROM email_campaigns` = 0 and `SELECT count(*) FROM email_campaign_recipients` = 0 — not 'zero pending', zero rows, ever. The handlers read exactly those tables: lib/jobs/handlers.ts:23 `case 'email_campaign_process' -> handleEmailCampaignProcess()` and :35 `case 'email_campaign_drain' -> handleEmailCampaignDrain()`, which at lib/jobs/handlers.ts:208-212 calls `drainCampaignRecipients()` from lib/services/campaign.service. Both are enqueued every tick at lib/jobs/index.ts:62-65 and :76-79. Measured over 24h: email_campaign_process 287 enqueued / 129 completed / 3,589 pending; email_campaign_drain 287 enqueued / 151 completed / 3,651 pending. Their job_logs cost is small individually (400 ms and 418 ms mean, 115 s/day combined) but they occupy 2 of the ~11 round-robin slots on every tick.
findings.impact: 574 job_queue rows minted per day (209,510/year) and 280 job executions/day for two features that have never been used once in production. 7,240 of the 19,006 pending rows (38%) belong to these two types. Every round-robin cycle in processJobBatch spends 2 of its ~11 turns and ~0.8 s of the 50 s budget on them, directly displacing types that do have work.
findings.recommendation: Gate the enqueue on the existence of work — `SELECT 1 FROM email_campaigns WHERE status IN ('sending','queued','scheduled') LIMIT 1` before calling safe() — or, since the feature is unbuilt, drop both from enqueueTimeBasedJobs entirely and re-add them when the first campaign is created. Then DELETE their 7,240 orphaned pending rows. This is independent of the dedup-key fix and both should be applied.

findings.title: 2.1 seconds of DB time is spent every tick deciding what to run, before any job executes — 62 hours/year of pure scheduling overhead
findings.evidence: pg_stat_statements (window since stats_reset 2026-05-07, 120 days), the three statements processJobBatch issues once per tick before any work: (1) `SELECT type, MAX(priority) AS priority FROM job_queue WHERE status=$1 AND run_at<=NOW() GROUP BY type ORDER BY priority DESC` (lib/jobs/db.ts:57, getDistinctPendingTypes) — 4,355 calls, mean 856.0 ms, max 3,158.2 ms, 10,614,521 blocks; (2) `SELECT type, COUNT(*)::text AS pending, (EXTRACT($1 FROM (NOW()-MIN(run_at)))/$2)::int::text AS oldest_mins FROM job_queue WHERE status=$3 AND run_at<=NOW() GROUP BY type` (getQueueDepth, called from emitQueueDepth at lib/jobs/processor.ts:145) — 603 calls, mean 1,259.5 ms, max 2,604.3 ms; (3) resetStuckJobs UPDATE — 8,335 calls, mean 5.9 ms. Sum of means = 2,121 ms per tick, x 288 ticks/day = 611 s/day = 62.0 h/year. Both scanning queries are O(pending backlog) — 19,006 rows — so the cost is a direct consequence of the enqueue-amplification finding.
findings.impact: 62 hours/year of database exec time spent on scheduling metadata, versus 4,384 s/day (~444 h/yr) of actual job work — so ~12% of all job-related DB time is the tick deciding what to do. Because these are the FIRST things a tick does, they also delay every job by ~2 s, which matters against a 50 s budget that only completes ~5 jobs.
findings.recommendation: Do not reduce the cron frequency to fix this — the queue is already arrival-bound and a 15-minute tick (96/day) would save 407 s/day of overhead but cut throughput by two thirds and deepen the backlog. Fix it upstream instead: after the dedup-key and dead-schedule fixes the backlog collapses from 19,006 to near zero and both queries become sub-10 ms index scans on idx_job_queue_pick. If the depth metric is still slow afterwards, downgrade emitQueueDepth from every tick to every 12th tick (hourly) — it is a monitoring read, and at 1,259.5 ms it is the most expensive single statement in the tick.

findings.title: mpesa_reconcile, mpesa_replay_callbacks and outbox_dispatch run every 5 minutes against lifetime volumes of 49, 81 and 33 rows
findings.evidence: Enqueued 287 times each per 24 h (lib/jobs/index.ts:133-136, :139-142, :145-148 — all with 5-minute time-bucketed dedup keys). Lifetime volume of everything they can act on, live prod: `SELECT count(*) FROM payments` = 49; `SELECT count(*) FROM mpesa_callbacks` = 81 (4 of which are known junk diagnostic rows); `SELECT count(*), count(*) FILTER (WHERE processed_at IS NULL) FROM event_outbox` = 33 total, 0 unprocessed. Their per-run cost is real: from job_logs over 24 h, mpesa_replay_callbacks avg 892 ms (127 s/day), mpesa_reconcile avg 1,039 ms (122 s/day), outbox_dispatch avg 390 ms (62 s/day) — 311 s/day combined. Cadence over the pg_cron lifetime is 105,120 runs/year per type against a payments table that has grown by 49 rows in total.
findings.impact: ~311 s/day of function and DB time, 861 job rows/day, and 3 of the ~11 round-robin slots on every tick, to re-check a payment spine that receives well under one event per day. outbox_dispatch is the clearest case: event_outbox is confirmed healthy at 33 rows / 0 unprocessed, yet it holds 2,091 pending job rows. These sweeps also sit at the top of the priority order (10, 9, 8), so they go first every round and consume budget before anything else.
findings.recommendation: Move all three to `if (fiveMinBucket === 0)` (hourly), alongside payment_orphan_monitor and disbursement_orphan_monitor which already run hourly at lib/jobs/index.ts:151-181. Saving: 861 -> 72 job rows/day (-789/day, -288k/year) and 311 -> 26 s/day of execution. Real-time payment responsiveness does not depend on these — inbound M-Pesa arrives via the registered /api/v1/daraja/c2b-confirm webhook, and these are backstop reconcilers. If 5-minute latency is genuinely wanted for mpesa_reconcile alone, keep that one at 5 min but give it the constant dedup key so it cannot accumulate.

findings.title: pgmq extension is installed with zero queues and zero code references, while a hand-rolled job_queue starves alongside it
findings.evidence: `SELECT extname, extversion FROM pg_extension` includes pgmq 1.5.1. `SELECT n.nspname, c.relname, pg_size_pretty(pg_total_relation_size(c.oid)) FROM pg_class c JOIN pg_namespace n ON n.oid=c.relnamespace WHERE n.nspname LIKE 'pgmq%' AND c.relkind IN ('r','p')` returns exactly one row — pgmq.meta, 16 kB — meaning no queue has ever been created (each pgmq queue would create its own q_*/a_* tables). `grep -rn 'pgmq' --include=*.ts --include=*.sql` across the repo (excluding node_modules) returns nothing.
findings.impact: Negligible in bytes, but it is a working queue implementation installed and forgotten while the application runs a hand-rolled job_queue that is 19,006 rows deep and cannot drain. It is misleading surface area for anyone auditing the scheduling stack, and an installed extension is a maintenance and upgrade obligation.
findings.recommendation: `DROP EXTENSION pgmq;` — it is provably unused. Do this as a deliberate decision, not a cleanup: if pgmq was installed as an intended replacement for job_queue, that intent is worth recording before removing it, because several of the findings above (round-robin fairness, stuck-job reset, dedup keys) are things pgmq gives for free.
